articles.title: In 2024, a Seattle-area homeowner learned a stranger had bought a five-foot-wide strip running through his backyard at a county auction
articles.summary: A Seattle-area homeowner was astonished to find out that a five-foot-wide strip running through his backyard had been purchased by a stranger at a county auction. Learn how this curious piece of land ended up being sold and what it means for property owners.
articles.body: Imagine discovering that a narrow strip of land running through your backyard belongs to a stranger. That was the surprise facing Harlen Ward, a homeowner in Auburn, Washington, after a stranger bought a five-foot-wide parcel of land between his property and a neighbour's at a King County auction. The strip stretched for about 300 feet and had no direct street access, making it hard to see how it could be used.According to Tribune News Service, Ward and his neighbour, Joe Hoeft, had long known that the unusual piece of land appeared on county maps. What they did not expect was for someone to purchase it. The parcel was eventually bought by Ben Harris, a California entrepreneur who specialises in buying unusual properties at county auctions and reselling them. Harris subsequently listed the narrow Auburn parcel for $3,950.How a strip of land ended up between homesThe five-foot-wide parcel was one of several unusual properties appearing in the Seattle region's county property system. According to King County, such "dangling strips" can be created because of errors in legal descriptions or surveys, subdivision mistakes, or mismeasurement by the county assessor's office. Some are only a few inches wide, while others extend considerable distances. In Ward's case, the parcel ran between his property and Hoeft's, surrounded by residential homes. Because it was only five feet wide and had no street access, it offered little obvious opportunity for construction.Research into urban vacant land has found that government parcel records can contain outdated information, transcription errors and incomplete details about a property's status or use. A study published in Landscape and Urban Planning also noted that vacant parcels can fall into categories including unusually shaped land and plots too small to be developed. These unusual parcels can therefore survive on official maps even when their practical purpose has become difficult to identify.The business behind unwanted landKing County’s process helps explain how land that neighbours saw as worthless could still attract a buyer. A piece of land can enter King County’s tax foreclosure program after property taxes go unpaid for some time. Properties that do not sell at the annual tax foreclosure sale may become what the county calls tax title properties. Many of them are described by the county as “dangling strips” or “isolated triangles,” as they are usually considered worthless since they did not fetch any bids during the previous auction.Harris’s strategy involved acquiring such odd parcels of land. According to reports, he had acquired at least 30 such parcels in King County since 2018 by paying only the back taxes on them. He would market some of these parcels to neighbouring homeowners or others who could find some practical use for them.His strategy was not limited to Auburn. The other plots of land that he bought included a tiny plot of driveway in the area of Seward Park in Seattle, and a small triangle of land bounded on all sides by properties in Mercer Island. These parcels could sell for several thousand dollars even though they offered little or no development potential. However, for a neighbour, there may be another advantage of purchasing a particular plot of land. Owning a strip of land could prevent an unknown person from controlling the land next to a homeowner’s property.Why these tiny parcels still matterKing County also says its property information is mainly used to calculate taxes and does not guarantee that land can be developed. They sell properties that are foreclosed for tax purposes, "as is." It encourages the buyer to do independent investigation. This is especially true when it comes to narrow pieces of land, like the piece passing through Ward's yard.Ward’s experience showed how a seemingly insignificant strip of land could have its own legal identity and be purchased by someone else. What appeared to be an ordinary part of his backyard was separately recorded as a parcel in the county’s property records. Auburn’s example shows how complicated property ownership can become even on a very small scale. A strip of land just five feet wide might be unsuitable for building and difficult to access, but it could still be legally owned by someone else if it was recorded as a separate parcel running through a homeowner’s property.You use AI every day. articles.title: NYC Episcopal priest sparks backlash after claiming God is nonbinary and Jesus 'transitioned' after resurrection
articles.summary: A NYC Episcopal priest, Father Flourish Klink, ignites fierce debate by asserting that God is nonbinary and suggesting Jesus was transgender. The comments, made during a sermon, have drawn backlash and concern from the Christian community.
articles.body: A New York City Episcopal priest has sparked a debate after claiming that God is nonbinary and suggesting that Jesus Christ was transgender.Father Flourish Klink, who is nonbinary and transgender, made the remarks during a sermon at Christ & St Stephen’s Episcopal Church on Manhattan’s Upper West Side. A clip from the sermon was shared on X on Wednesday.“God is nonbinary,” Klink said. “But I’m going to go further than that, and I’m going to say God is actually also trans.”Klink compared the experience of transgender people with the way Jesus was identified as a boy at birth. He argued that people are assigned a gender based on what others see when they are born, but may later realise that the assigned gender does not reflect who they are.Klink applied that argument to Jesus, saying Mary would have identified him as a boy when he was born. At the same time, God, in their interpretation, exists beyond the categories of male and female.“God was assigned a gender at birth, and later on it became clear that that gender wasn’t right,” Klink said.He then pointed to accounts of Jesus after his resurrection, when his disciples did not immediately recognise him.“The Bible doesn’t tell us why it is that Jesus’ best friends, his disciples, the people who had walked with him to the end of his life, the people who had buried him in the tomb when it was politically difficult, who were committed to him still didn’t recognise Jesus for a good long time,” Klink said.Klink acknowledged that the explanation was based on personal interpretation rather than certainty“Now I don’t know for sure, I wasn’t there,” Klink said.“But based on everything else I know about God, I have an idea. I think Jesus was resurrected as Jesus’ true self, which is beyond male or female. I think Jesus was not only transfigured; I think Jesus transitioned.”Klink also argued that Jesus did not follow what they described as the traditional life of a first-century man. He pointed to his decision not to marry and his interactions with women, which Klink said differed from traditionally masculine behaviour.The remarks drew criticism online, with commenters questioning the priest’s interpretation of Jesus and the church’s decision to allow the sermon.One commenter wrote: “Has Christianity become this useless that Christians would openly blaspheme against Jesus Christ like this & Christians would allow it, they’re not demanding that demon-possessed scammer be stripped of their title & position in the church? articles.title: 160 years ago, a ship caught fire and ran aground off Australia; now, mangroves have turned it into a living island filled with greenery and wildlife
articles.summary: Built in Glasgow in the 1860s, the City of Adelaide began life as an iron-hulled passenger and mail steamer before undergoing several transformations that
articles.body: Built in Glasgow in the 1860s, the City of Adelaide began life as an iron-hulled passenger and mail steamer before undergoing several transformations that eventually left it stranded off Magnetic Island in Queensland. After becoming a coal-storage hulk, the vessel was badly damaged by fire in 1912 and later bought with plans to give it another purpose as a breakwater or tourist accommodation. Instead, it ran aground at Cockle Bay in 1916 and remained there. More than a century later, the rusting remains have become intertwined with mangroves growing around and through the wreck. The ship's transformation from working passenger vessel to vegetation-covered wreck has made it a distinctive part of Magnetic Island's maritime and natural landscape.The ship that caught fire and ran aground off AustraliaThe City of Adelaide was launched in 1863 and completed in 1864 by J&G Thomson in Glasgow, Scotland. The iron-hulled vessel was built for passenger and cargo services and operated between Australian ports, including Melbourne and Sydney. It later served as a mail steamer on routes that extended to New Zealand, Honolulu and San Francisco. In 1890, its steam machinery was removed and the vessel was converted into a four-masted sailing ship. By 1902, it had become a coal-storage hulk at Townsville. Its working life changed dramatically again in 1912, when its coal cargo caught fire and the vessel was badly damaged.A burned-out vessel was meant to become a breakwaterAfter the fire, the damaged vessel was bought by George Butler, a Magnetic Island businessman, in 1915. Butler had plans for the old ship that would have given it a very different final chapter. Proposals included using it as tourist accommodation or incorporating it into a breakwater and jetty at Picnic Bay. The plan, however, never reached its intended destination. While the vessel was being towed towards Magnetic Island, it ran aground at Cockle Bay in 1916. The ship was never refloated and remained in the shallow coastal waters, where its exposed hull gradually deteriorated.The wreck became part of Magnetic Island lifeThe abandoned vessel eventually became more than a maritime relic. ABC reported that by the 1920s, people were visiting the wreck, with swimmers reportedly using it as a changing room and collecting oysters that grew around the structure. The City of Adelaide also acquired a wartime connection. In 1942, a Royal Australian Air Force aircraft struck one of the wreck's masts during a training exercise, killing four people aboard the aircraft. Decades later, Cyclone Althea in 1971 caused further damage to the already deteriorating wreck. These events left the remains in increasingly fragmented condition, but substantial sections of the historic iron vessel continued to survive in Cockle Bay.Mangroves have grown through the century-old wreckOver the decades, the coastal environment has increasingly become part of the wreck itself. Mangroves now grow around and through sections of the rusting iron structure, giving the remains an unusual appearance from the air and making the wreck resemble a small vegetated island. The Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority identifies the City of Adelaide as one of the historic wrecks around Magnetic Island and notes the ecological role that shipwrecks can play by providing surfaces and structure for marine organisms. ABC has also reported that expanding mangrove growth around Cockle Bay has made the wreck increasingly difficult to see from land. The result is a striking combination of maritime history and coastal vegetation, rather than a conventional shipwreck sitting alone in open water.The 160-year-old wreck is now part of a coastal ecosystemThe City of Adelaide lies about 300 metres offshore at Cockle Bay in relatively shallow water and can be approached by wading at low tide under suitable conditions. Its mangrove-covered remains now form part of the coastal environment, where vegetation and marine organisms occupy the structure. However, describing it as a literal natural island can be misleading: it remains a shipwreck, with mangroves growing on and around its surviving sections. The Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority treats historic wrecks as maritime heritage and advises visitors not to remove, disturb or interfere with artefacts. More than a century after the City of Adelaide ran aground, its rusting remains have therefore taken on a new role, with nature gradually reshaping a once-working ship into a distinctive green landmark in Queensland's coastal landscape.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Long Island credit supervisor used his access to customer accounts to divert about $1.6 million over four years; prosecutors say the money funded a failed restaurant venture, wedding expenses and travel
articles.summary: For four years, a credit supervisor at a Long Island health care products company had access to a pool of money intended for customer refunds.
articles.body: For four years, a credit supervisor at a Long Island health care products company had access to a pool of money intended for customer refunds. Federal prosecutors say he quietly redirected that access for himself, moving about $1.6 million into an account he controlled and disguising the transfers as legitimate refunds. The scheme eventually came to an end in federal court, where Tony Ream, 35, was sentenced to 30 months in prison for wire fraud. He was also ordered to repay the full $1.6 million and pay a $1,000 fine, states an online report by the United States Attorney's Office.How the scheme workedAs per the website, Ream joined the Melville-based company in 2019 and eventually became a supervisor in its credit department. The company distributes health care products and services to dental and medical practitioners around the world. According to court filings and statements made during the proceedings, Ream began diverting corporate funds in approximately October 2020. He sought out customer refund accounts, including inactive ones, and funneled money from these accounts into a bank account that he controlled. These transfers were then recorded as customer refunds, making it appear that the money had been properly refunded to customers. The arrangement continued until November 2024. Over that period, prosecutors determined that approximately $1.6 million had been taken from the company.Subordinates were drawn into the processThe scheme did not operate entirely on Ream’s actions alone. Prosecutors said he deceived employees who reported to him into taking steps that ultimately helped facilitate the transfers. Because the transactions were made to look like ordinary customer refunds, the activity could be concealed within the company’s financial processes for an extended period. The case centered on Ream’s access to company accounts and his ability to manipulate refund transactions as part of his position in the credit department, adds the online report.Where the money wentThe stolen funds were used for a range of personal expenses, according to federal prosecutors. Some of the money financed Ream’s wedding, while additional funds went toward luxury international travel. A substantial portion was also used in connection with a restaurant venture in South Carolina that ultimately failed. The spending turned company funds intended for customers into personal financing for a lifestyle and business venture unrelated to Ream’s employment.Prison and restitutionReam pleaded guilty to wire fraud in September before being sentenced by US District Judge Sanket J. Bulsara in federal court in Central Islip. His sentence includes 30 months of imprisonment, followed by an order to pay $1.6 million in restitution to the company. He was also assessed a $1,000 fine. The case was prosecuted by the US Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of New York, with assistance from the FBI’s New York Field Office.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: 'Could endanger his life': Imran Khan's son warns against Adiala jail protest
articles.summary: Former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan's son Kasim Khan has urged Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) supporters not to march towards Rawalpindi's Adiala
articles.body: Former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan's son Kasim Khan has urged Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) supporters not to march towards Rawalpindi's Adiala jail during the party's planned September 27 protest, warning that such a move could be used by Pakistani authorities as a pretext for a "counter" assault on the prison and put his father's life at risk.The warning comes ahead of the PTI's planned protest and march, which is being held to demand Imran Khan's release.The former premier has been in prison since August 2023 following convictions in multiple cases.In a post on X, Kasim said he had been asked to appeal to supporters against gathering near Adiala jail."I’ve been instructed to call on the public not to attempt to march or protest nearby Adiala jail on 27. I’ve heard from sources that this may be used as an excuse for the establishment to launch a “counter” assault on the jail (Which my father is being held in), which could endanger his life. Please do not give them any reasons for “accidents” to happen to my father during the protest," Kasim's post read.His appeal comes as security measures have been stepped up across Punjab ahead of the PTI mobilisation.The Punjab government has imposed Section 144 across the province from September 23 to October 5, restricting public gatherings of five or more people on roads and in public places. Authorities have also sought the deployment of Pakistan Rangers in Rawalpindi, Attock, Jhelum and Mianwali.The restrictions have been imposed citing security concerns. A provincial notification referred to a "serious and imminent threat" to public peace and safety from militant and terrorist organisations and hostile intelligence agencies.The planned protest comes amid the detention of three of Imran Khan's sisters. Aleema Khan was detained last week, followed by Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi, who were detained for 30 days under the Punjab maintenance of public order ordinance.On Thursday, the Lahore high court refused to immediately suspend the detention orders against Uzma and Noreen. The court issued notices to the respondents and sought their replies before taking up the plea further.The detentions have added to tensions ahead of the September 27 mobilisation.According to Dawn, lawyers for Uzma and Noreen told the Lahore high court that the two women were "non-political" and had been detained without sufficient legal justification. The court decided to wait for the authorities' response before ruling on their request to suspend the detention orders.Kasim had earlier criticised the detention of his aunts and other relatives and called for international attention to the issue.“This is a disgrace. Now my Aunts Dr. Uzma and Noreen, along with my cousins Shershah and Shahrez, have now been abducted as well. They have broken into my aunties' and cousins' houses and forced them into vehicles with no explanation. No reasons for arrest have been stated," he said in a post on X.Pakistani authorities have said the preventive detentions and restrictions are linked to public-order and security concerns. The Punjab government's notification specifically cited threats from militant organisations and other security risks while announcing the province-wide restrictions.The September 27 PTI protest is expected to add to the political and security pressure surrounding Imran Khan's continued incarceration, with authorities tightening restrictions and increasing security in areas linked to the planned mobilisation.You use AI every day. articles.title: He gave away 80% of his income, taught in an African school with just one computer: How Peter Tabichi became the ‘world’s best teacher’ and won $1 million
articles.summary: A science teacher in rural Kenya was giving away most of his monthly income to help poor families and students.
articles.body: A science teacher in rural Kenya was giving away most of his monthly income to help poor families and students. At the same time, he was teaching in a school with one computer, poor internet access and limited facilities. His students, however, were competing against some of the country's better-equipped schools in science competitions. In 2019, that teacher, Peter Tabichi, was named the winner of the $1 million Global Teacher Prize, becoming the first African winner of the award.Tabichi taught mathematics and physics at Keriko Mixed Day Secondary School in Pwani Village, in Kenya's Rift Valley. The school was in a remote, semi-arid area where drought and food insecurity were recurring problems. According to the official website of the Global Teacher Prize, about 95% of the students came from poor families, while almost a third were orphans or had only one parent.He gave away 80% of his incomeAccording to the official website of the Global Teacher Prize, Tabichi was a member of the Franciscan religious order and donated 80% of his monthly income to help poor people in his community. He used his income to support people facing financial difficulties, while he also spent additional time helping students who were struggling academically. He and four other teachers provided one-to-one tuition in mathematics and science outside regular school hours, including on weekends. Speaking to The National after winning the award, Tabichi said he had been donating 80% of his salary since joining the Franciscan order. “They come from very poor families, even affording breakfast is hard. When they are in school they are not able to concentrate mainly because they are not able to get enough meals at home,” Tabichi said.The school had one computerAs reported by The Global Teacher Prize, Keriko Mixed Day Secondary School did not have the facilities available in many better-resourced schools. The school had just one computer, poor internet connectivity and a student-teacher ratio of 58:1. Students also had to walk several kilometres to reach the school. Yet Tabichi incorporated technology into his teaching wherever he could. The Global Teacher Prize said he used ICT in about 80% of his lessons, sometimes visiting internet cafés and saving online material so it could be used offline in class. Tabichi himself believed that limited resources could make creativity more important, rather than less. “Creativity is very important, especially in challenging situations and resource constrained environments,” he told The National. “To be a great teacher, you have to be creative and use technology, you really have to promote those modern ways of teaching. You have to do more and talk less.”His students started winning science competitionsOne of Tabichi's biggest achievements was helping students discover an interest in science and turn it into practical projects. He expanded the school's Science Club and helped students develop research projects. According to the Global Teacher Prize, around 60% of the students involved in the programme qualified for national competitions. In the 2018 Kenya Science and Engineering Fair, his students presented a device designed to help blind and deaf people measure objects. The school went on to finish first nationally in the public schools category. Another student team developed a project using local plants to generate electricity and received recognition from the Royal Society of Chemistry."I am only here because of what my students have achieved”Tabichi's work eventually took him far beyond his school in rural Kenya. In March 2019, he was announced as the winner of the Global Teacher Prize, selected from around 10,000 applicants from 179 countries, according to The Guardian. The award was presented at a ceremony in Dubai hosted by actor Hugh Jackman. Tabichi became the first African winner of the prize. But in his acceptance speech, Tabichi shifted the attention away from himself. “I am only here because of what my students have achieved. This prize gives them a chance. It tells the world that they can do anything,” he said. He also said: “Every day in Africa we turn a new page and a new chapter ... This prize does not recognise me but recognises this great continent's young people.” The award also came with $1 million in prize money.He wanted the prize money to help his communityTabichi said he wanted to use the prize money to improve the facilities available to his students and help his wider community. Speaking to The National, he said he wanted to build a modern school laboratory and develop projects that could help people deal with food insecurity, including kitchen gardening and drought-resistant crops. For Tabichi, the prize was therefore not simply recognition for his own work. He saw it as an opportunity for his students and community. “I know this is the beginning of a new life not just for me but for Kenya and Africa,” he told The National after receiving the award. He also summed up his approach to teaching in simple terms: “Seeing my learners grow in knowledge, skills and confidence is my greatest joy in teaching!” the Global Teacher Prize quoted him as saying.Where is Peter Tabichi now?Peter Tabichi is now working full-time with the Peter Tabichi Foundation, where he serves as its founder and programme lead. The foundation works with teachers across Kenya to develop practical, inclusive and curriculum-aligned teaching resources and build professional learning communities. According to the Global Teacher Prize, Tabichi completed a Master of Arts in Education and International Development from University College London, which he pursued part-time while continuing his work as a teacher and contributing to education reform in Kenya.You use AI every day. articles.title: A painting seized from a Munich banker’s widow during Nazi persecution has been returned to her US heirs after decades of uncertainty; provenance researchers traced the 1892 work through wartime records and museum archives
articles.summary: More than eight decades after Nazi persecution tore a painting from the home of Sofie Heilbronner, the 19th-century work has finally returned to her
articles.body: More than eight decades after Nazi persecution tore a painting from the home of Sofie Heilbronner, the 19th-century work has finally returned to her family. Its journey from a Munich warehouse to a Bavarian state collection and, eventually, to Heilbronner’s heirs in the United States reflects the long and painstaking process of tracing art displaced during the Nazi eral, states an online report by Pinakothek website. The restitution was marked by a ceremony at the German Embassy in Washington, DC, on September 22, 2026, attended by descendants of Heilbronner.A painting lost to historyHeilbronner, the widow of a Munich banker, lost the work as a result of racial persecution under the Nazi regime. After the war, its whereabouts remained unclear for decades, leaving the ownership history unresolved. The painting, created in 1892, eventually surfaced in the holdings of the Bavarian State Painting Collections. In 2015, the institution published information about the work on the Lost Art database because its provenance raised the possibility that it had been looted or otherwise displaced during the Nazi period. That public record became an important first step toward determining who had originally owned the painting and how it entered the state collection.Records reveal the missing trailA more detailed provenance investigation began in 2020 through the Provenance Research Department of the Bavarian Museum Agency. Researchers reconstructed part of the painting’s wartime journey and established that it had been transported from a warehouse on Munich’s Lazarettstrasse. It was subsequently taken into the state system through what was described at the time as a transfer of state-owned property by the Bavarian State Office of Asset Management and Restitution.As per the report, the investigation helped establish that the painting had been seized from Heilbronner in connection with Nazi persecution rather than entering the state collection through an ordinary purchase or legitimate transfer.Evidence from historic galleriesA breakthrough came through records from two prominent Munich art dealers, Galerie Heinemann and Galerie Hugo Helbing.The documents provided crucial evidence linking the 1892 painting to Heilbronner and helped confirm her as its former rightful owner. Such gallery records can be particularly valuable in provenance investigations because they preserve information about sales, consignments and previous owners that may otherwise have disappeared from the historical record.In 2021, the New York State Department of Financial Services Holocaust Claims Processing Office contacted the Bavarian State Painting Collections on behalf of Heilbronner’s heirs after the provenance information and Lost Art listing had been made public.A family connection restoredAs per the same report, the return closes a decades-long gap in the history of a painting that had been separated from its rightful family during one of the darkest periods of European history. It also demonstrates why provenance research remains essential for museums holding works whose ownership histories intersect with the Nazi era. Piecing together old gallery records, government documents, wartime inventories and museum archives can take years, but each discovery can help resolve ownership questions that have remained unanswered for generations.For Heilbronner’s descendants, the restitution brings a tangible part of their family history back into their hands. For researchers and museums, the case adds another documented chapter to the continuing effort to identify and return art displaced through Nazi persecution.Image Courtesy: Pinakothek websiteYou use AI every day. articles.title: Trump's 48 F-35 jets for Saudi Arabia: Why is Israel uneasy and China a key concern
articles.summary: The Trump administration has agreed to put the world's most advanced combat aircraft in Saudi hands.
articles.body: The Trump administration has agreed to put the world's most advanced combat aircraft in Saudi hands. It comes at a time when Gulf allies are questioning whether American primacy still carries weight. And nowhere is that question more important than in the ever-conflicted region of West Asia.Washington's approach to West Asia has long resembled digging a hole to bury sand, only to be left with a new heap of sand, creating a loop that keeps the digging going.Trump's decision to approve the $24.3 billion sale of F-35s to the Saudis, when the Kingdom is being bogged down by the Iran-backed Houthis, appears to be the latest turn of the spade.Though it is meant to steady a Gulf partner shaken by Iranian fire and doubts about American guarantees, the aircraft deal has opened a fresh cavity for Israel, until now the only country in the region to fly the world's most powerful combat aircraft.Under the deal, the state department has notified Congress of a possible sale of 48 jets, with engines and support, which would make Saudi Arabia the second country in the Middle East to fly the aircraft after Israel. However, the Saudi jets will reportedly not have all the advanced features of the F-35s operated by Israel.The F-35I, also known as the Adir, a custom variant based on the Alpha, redesigned, and modified by the Israeli Defence Force (IDF). Although strictly forbidden, after negotiations the US defence force reluctantly gave permission for Israeli designers to make certain modifications to the F-35A design.Production and delivery would take years, but the political signal is immediate, with some Israeli officials raising concerns that the deal could erode their country's "qualitative military edge" -- a standard that American policymakers have sought to protect since the 1973 war and that Congress has mandated.Numbers not the real worryIsrael bought 50 F-35s in two rounds, in 2016 and 2017, although several reports suggest two have yet to arrive. That leaves 48 on the ground, the same number Riyadh has requested.However, Israel will not stay level for long, since its defence ministry plans 25 more jets from 2028 and has announced a further squadron of unspecified size.The anxiety is therefore about something less measurable. When Donald Trump first confirmed he was considering the sale last November, Israeli officials told Axios they did not oppose it as such, but wanted it "to be subject to Saudi normalisation with Israel". That condition has not been met, and no such deal appears close.A security source told CNN at the time that Saudi Arabia acquiring "the same capabilities" was "very concerning". Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, however, reportedly played down its significance.Meanwhile, Washington has maintained that regional balance will hold as "the proposed sale of this equipment and support will not alter the military balance in the region". Interestingly, whether Israel accepts that assurance will depend less on the wording than on who Riyadh chooses to stand with in the years ahead.China's shadow over the dealThe strongest objection in Washington concerns Beijing, with a defense intelligence agency assessment, issued months ago, questioning whether American and Saudi personnel could secure the sites that would hold F-35 technology.It also flagged the access Chinese military personnel have to Saudi bases and the kingdom's heavy use of Chinese telecommunications technology in its infrastructure and defence installations.An earlier assessment had already questioned the growing partnership, in which China sells Saudi Arabia ballistic missiles and helps it learn to build them.Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi, a Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, put the fear plainly. "It could put the crown jewels of American military technology within reach of the Chinese Communist Party," he said.There is also a precedent when Trump announced an F-35 sale to the United Arab Emirates (UAE) in 2020, and the Biden administration ended the process over similar worries about Abu Dhabi's links with China.For Israel, the risk is indirect; it's highly unlikely that Riyadh, which is absorbing Iranian missile and drone attacks, would hand secrets to Tehran.The concern is leakage through third parties. The US intelligence agencies worry that Chinese spies could target Saudi networks, maintenance sites and personnel, a task made easier by Chinese military personnel's access to Saudi bases and by Chinese technology in the Kingdom's telecommunications and defence installations.The burden of broken promisesUnderstanding why Riyadh might gradually hedge against America in the future, potentially against Israel's interests, helps trace how American security promises have fared over the years.The 2003 invasion of Iraq, launched with great confidence in what military force could achieve, ended in a costly occupation and shook the regional order, though that order eventually reassembled.In 2011, the fall of Egypt's Hosni Mubarak convinced Arab autocrats they could not count on Washington to save them from domestic upheaval. Several set out to contain threats themselves, often with devastating results.Doubts about deterrence against Iran grew denser after Washington did not respond to a 2019 attack on Saudi oil refineries attributed to Iran, and Houthi drone strikes on the UAE in 2022 deepened the unease.The 2026 war with Iran did the most damage as Gulf leaders were seemingly angry that the United States and Israel launched it without consulting them, in the middle of Omani-brokered talks with Tehran.Iran struck every Gulf state but concentrated on Bahrain and the UAE, both Abraham Accords signatories. Missile defences stopped the worst, yet enough got through to cause real harm, and much of the network of American bases was damaged, destroyed or rendered irrelevant.Washington then failed to dislodge the Iranian regime and could not keep the Strait of Hormuz open. American strikes on Iranian water storage facilities, and Israeli strikes on oil depots, alarmed Gulf capitals that feared reprisals against their own water and nuclear sites.Even Riyadh's long-sought nuclear agreement was left in limbo when Trump changed its terms a day after it was finalised.Moreover, Mohammed bin Salman, the Kingdom's Crown Prince, is reportedly unhappy with Trump's refusal to provide direct military support to Saudi Arabia in its fight against the Houthis. Particarly after the its key East-West oil pipeline was hit in the attack.That makes the F-35 deal look less like a favour and more like a transaction, which Trump has ensured with all his key allies, even Europe.Summing up that sentiment, retired US Lieutenant General Karen Gibson put it aptly: "MBS will not forget."The rival camp Riyadh has been buildingBefore the fighting began at the end of February, Saudi Arabia had started assembling a bloc of its own. Riyadh drew Egypt, Pakistan, Qatar and Turkey into a coalition meant to counter the American-backed Emirati-Israeli alliance.This matters a great deal for the F-35 question. The country due to receive the aircraft that anchors Israel's air power has been organising against an alignment that includes Israel.Also, Riyadh's rivalry with Abu Dhabi runs deep. Saudi Arabia backs the post-Assad government in Syria, while the UAE shares Israel's hostility towards it. In Yemen, Riyadh recently drove out Emirati proxies, and it has complained that the UAE promotes secessionist movements that undermine regional stability.Also, the UAE coordinated with Israel and the United States on strikes against Iranian targets. Riyadh watches that alignment uneasily, seeing it as a threat to its own leadership.Turkey adds another layer as Netanyahu has already called President Recep Tayyip Erdogan "not exactly a model ally of the United States", a remark he made after Trump said in July that he was weighing F-35 sales to Ankara as well. Israel thus faces advanced American jets flowing to more than one capital whose interests diverge from its own.Why Israel worriesArab allies who have lost faith in Washington, sooner or later, will increasingly exercise their autonomy, which could mean diplomacy with Iran and closer ties with China and Russia, whatever American officials prefer.Saudi Arabia has precedent here, having reached a rapprochement with Iran in 2023. Some Gulf states may now seek side deals with Tehran to stay off its target list. For a kingdom under Iranian fire, that is prudence rather than defection.Yet a fifth-generation fleet needs decades of spares, software and training, so it presumes a buyer whose alignment stays put. None of this points to an imminent break, and Gulf states may even deepen ties with Washington in the short term. A Saudi Arabia that talks to Tehran, buys Chinese missiles and uses Chinese telecommunications networks is a partner whose direction Israel cannot easily read.Congress has been given 30 days to review the sale and could pass a joint resolution of disapproval, but it would need two-thirds of both chambers to survive a veto. The House is in recess until November and the Senate is about to follow, so blocking the sale looks improbable. Any safeguards will have to be secured well before delivery.Saudi Arabia, under fire, remains by far the biggest buyer of American weapons, and interoperability with US and allied forces has genuine value.But the deeper question is whether an advanced weapon, under a purely transactional agreement, can secure loyalty against the backdrop of wobbling US guarantees? That, more than any tally of jets, is what perhaps unsettles Israel.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Volunteers reveal 2,000-year-old Iron Age Deepdale Bridge Settlement in England's Lake District, revealing roundhouses occupied into the Roman era
articles.summary: A group of 25 dedicated volunteers has revealed a rare Iron Age settlement in the Deepdale valley of the Lake District National Park.
articles.body: A group of 25 dedicated volunteers has revealed a rare Iron Age settlement in the Deepdale valley of the Lake District National Park. The find, known as the Deepdale Bridge Settlement, emerged as part of a wider survey of 150 sites in the valley that began in 2024, carried out with support from landowners Jimmy and Chris Brown, the Lake District National Park Authority, and Eden Heritage. Here's what the volunteers found, and what it reveals about life in the ancient Lake District.25 volunteers uncover the Deepdale Bridge SettlementAccording to the Lake District National Park Authority, the settlement comprises several hut circles, the remains of roundhouses, and small enclosures surrounded by a rubble bank, where ancient communities would have lived, cooked together and kept livestock. Very few native enclosed settlements of this kind have been archaeologically investigated in the Lake District, and even fewer have confirmed occupation dates, making the excavation a significant contribution to understanding the region's ancient historical landscape. Marnie Calvert, Graduate Historic Environment Assistant, credited the volunteers directly, saying their dedication, enthusiasm and hard work had been at the heart of this excavation uncovering important new evidence of life in the later prehistoric Lake District.What the roundhouse and enclosure revealedOne trench dug during the excavation revealed the remains of a timber doorway leading into the roundhouse, along with internal dividers and a cobbled yard outside that was probably used to hold animals. The roundhouse had also been altered throughout its life, demonstrating the continual use and reuse of the settlement over time. Evidence of spelt wheat and barley points to an active farming community living in the Deepdale landscape into the Roman period, suggesting the settlement remained in use as communities adapted to changing conditions.Radiocarbon dating the settlement's occupationCharcoal recovered from the soil was radiocarbon dated, revealing that the roundhouse was occupied between 76 and 216 AD. The enclosure bank was constructed between 40 BC and 118 AD. Together, the dates indicate that the settlement was in use across the transition from the late Iron Age into the Roman period. Martin Railton, archaeological consultant for Eden Heritage and volunteer leader, said, "We know surprisingly little about the people who lived here and farmed the landscape in prehistory," adding that the investigation would help shed light on several other settlements likely dating to the same period.What's next for Lake District archaeology volunteersVolunteer Siriol Hinchcliffe reflected on the project, telling the Lake District National Park Authority, "Our team of volunteers have spent two years surveying in the valley and being able to excavate to further our knowledge is great." With the potential to uncover much more about the region's ancient history, volunteers are now preparing for a 2026 excavation at Lanthwaite Green near Crummock Water.You use AI every day. articles.title: Called ‘black-complexioned’ and ‘fatty-shaped’: Why man’s divorce plea failed
articles.summary: BILASPUR: Calling a husband “black complexioned” or “fatty shaped” may be hurtful, but such remarks alone cannot constitute sufficient grounds for
articles.body: BILASPUR: Calling a husband “black complexioned” or “fatty shaped” may be hurtful, but such remarks alone cannot constitute sufficient grounds for divorce, the Chhattisgarh high court has held while dismissing a man's appeal seeking to end his marriage.The court said the husband had failed to substantiate his allegations of cruelty and desertion against his wife with sufficient evidence.A division bench of Justice Parth Prateem Sahu and Justice Sachin Singh Rajput was hearing the man's appeal against a family court order that had rejected his plea for divorce and directed him to return his wife's stridhan.The couple had married on March 7, 2019. The husband alleged that his wife behaved in a hostile manner, threatened to implicate him and frequently went to her parental home.He also claimed that she left him after returning from Rajasthan and refused to resume their marriage despite his efforts to bring her back.He relied on the fact that his wife had been living separately since December 2019 and had initiated proceedings under the Domestic Violence Act against him and his family.The wife denied the allegations. She claimed that her husband was in an illicit relationship with another woman, had started consuming alcohol and abused her.She also alleged that he did not properly care for her during her pregnancy and that her mother had taken her to Raigarh for treatment when she fell ill.The high court examined the evidence and found that the husband's allegations were not supported by sufficient proof.“Though the appellant/husband has made several allegations against the respondent/wife yet none of them have been substantiated by leading any cogent evidence of the witnesses. Of course, he has alleged that the respondent/wife used to brand him as being a black complexioned or a fatty shaped but they cannot be taken to be sufficient ground for granting a decree of divorce to him.”The court also considered the circumstances cited by the husband regarding the wife's stay away from him. It noted that the wife had said she had gone to Rajasthan to attend a relative's marriage along with her husband, mother-in-law and mother. The court also found that when she fell ill, her husband had taken her for treatment before her mother took her to Raigarh.On the allegation of desertion, the bench said the husband had failed to establish that his wife was staying with her parents without a reasonable excuse.It noted evidence suggesting that members of the husband's family had sent her away with her mother after her miscarriage.The court referred to the Supreme Court's decision in Samar Ghosh vs Jaya Ghosh, which laid down illustrative instances relevant to determining mental cruelty in matrimonial disputes. It said the circumstances in the present case did not bring the wife's conduct within that category.The bench also said that merely making several allegations could not justify divorce when those allegations were not backed by evidence.“May be, the allegations are many in number by the appellant/husband but in the absence of any pinpointed evidence to substantiate the same, they cannot be made basis for granting decree of divorce in his favour. As regards the element of cruelty at the hands of respondent/wife, the elements required to constitute the same appear to be totally amiss.”The court further found that the husband had failed to establish the intention required to prove desertion. It noted that the wife and her mother had consistently stated that he had not made efforts to take her back after she went to her parental home.The high court therefore found no reason to interfere with the family court's decision.The bench dismissed the husband's appeal seeking divorce, upheld the finding that cruelty and desertion had not been proved and also upheld the direction to return the wife's stridhan given by her parents.The appeal was dismissed without imposing any costs.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Raipur | Silver Rate in Raipur | Bank Holidays in Raipur | Public Holidays in Raipur | Raipur AQI | Weather in Raipur | Petrol Price in Raipur | Diesel Price in Raipur | CNG Price in Raipur | LPG Price in RaipurStay updated with the latest Raipur news. articles.summary: BENGALURU: A local court in Bengaluru Friday rejected the bail petition of IAS officer Gyanendra Kumar Gangwar, 41, arrested and imprisoned in the alleged
articles.body: BENGALURU: A local court in Bengaluru Friday rejected the bail petition of IAS officer Gyanendra Kumar Gangwar, 41, arrested and imprisoned in the alleged job for cash scam at Karnataka Public Service Commission (KPSC).On Tuesday, the same court had turned down the bail petition of another accused in the case-Basavaraj Kannale.Gyanendra's counsel had argued that the suspended IAS officer is suffering from testicular cancer and needs rest."Gyanendra is a survivor of testicular cancer undergone two surgeries and still under going chemotherapy. Also, he suffers from life threatening medical conditions and high blood pressure, asthma and chronic liver condition. The MRI scan conducted at Victoria hospital on September 3 revealed severe lumbar spinal degeneration in L3-L4 and L4-L5 regions, for which doctors have advised immediate spinal surgery and complete bed rest," counsel noted.However, public prosecutor Bhagyalakshmi KL had objected to the petition stating accused is an IAS officer and could threaten the witnesses besides tampering the investigation."Gyanendra, an influential person, is arraigned as accused number five in the case and if bail is granted he will influence the further investigation. CID police has identified the place where Gyanendra had given question papers to another accused Basavaraj Kannale; also, police have discovered that Xiamoi Tab used for the commission of offence has been destroyed," Bhagyalakshmi said.She further argued, "The accused Basavaraj Kannale had collected the money from the candidates by way of deposit through Om Lakshmi Souharda Co-operative Society Ltd and through one Balu reddy. Thereafter he used the said money for his personal use and also transferred the said money to Bhima Jewellers situated at Commercial Street, Bengaluru for the purpose of purchasing gold jewels by Gyanendra.""CID police have seized gold jewelleries and investigating further regarding there is remaining golden ornaments if concealed by Gyanendra. Also, police has identified the person who assisted Basavaraj Kannale for the com mission of alleged offence has been identified and investigation is going on. Police has seized NVR (Net work Video recording) regarding Kannale visiting Gyanendra's house," public prosecutor added.Bhagyalakshmi further argued, "The investigation regarding forensic analysis of digital equipments seized is still pending. articles.title: Govt frames draft rules for pedestrian safety
articles.summary: Odisha issues draft Pedestrian Safety Rules 2026: mandatory footpaths, safer crossings, school zone speed limits, anti-encroachment steps; 30-day feedback window.
articles.body: Bhubaneswar: Odisha govt has framed draft rules to improve pedestrian safety across the state, proposing mandatory footpaths, safer crossings, stricter enforcement against encroachments and protection of vulnerable road users. It came in the wake of Supreme Court’s ruling in June that citizens have a “fundamental right to walk” and require safe pedestrian infrastructure.The proposed Odisha Pedestrian Safety Rules-2026 were issued by the commerce and transport department on Thursday, inviting public objections and suggestions for 30 days before finalisation. According to Odisha police data, altogether 735 pedestrians, including 143 women, were killed in accidents in Odisha in 2024.“Under the draft rules, priority will be given to developing pedestrian-friendly zones around schools, hospitals, markets, bus stops, transit terminals, govt offices, pilgrimage and tourist destinations, industrial areas and high-crash locations, besides places where pedestrian deaths or injuries have been reported in the past two to three years,” a senior official said.School zones will have advance warning signs, road markings, speed-limit signs, traffic-calming measures, pedestrian crossings, footpaths, safe waiting areas and regulated pick-up and drop-off points.“The maximum speed in school zones on urban roads and rural built-up roads will ordinarily be capped at 25 kmph. On highways or major rural roads adjoining schools, it may be fixed at up to 40 kmph, subject to traffic-calming measures, warning signs and safe crossings,” the draft rules proposed.The draft also proposes bollards, kerbs and guardrails to prevent vehicles from accessing footpaths, while ensuring that such measures do not hinder wheelchair users. Braille markings will also have to be provided on ramps or stair handrails where applicable. The rules prohibit utilities, landscaping, street furniture, signboards, advertisements and temporary structures from being placed in the clear walking zone.Footpaths will also have to be connected with bus stops, railway stations, transit hubs, public bicycle-sharing stations, cycle stands and other transport facilities to ensure safe first- and last-mile connectivity.The draft rules further mandate that every road project carry a signed declaration from the engineer-in-charge and contractor certifying compliance with pedestrian safety standards.If an investigation establishes that failure by a road-owning agency, contractor or consultant to comply with prescribed design, construction or maintenance standards caused or contributed to a death or disability, action may be initiated against those responsible.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Bhubaneswar | Silver Rate in Bhubaneswar | Bank Holidays in Bhubaneswar | Public Holidays in Bhubaneswar | Petrol Price in Bhubaneswar | Diesel Price in Bhubaneswar | CNG Price in Bhubaneswar | LPG Price in BhubaneswarStay updated with the latest Bhubaneswar news. articles.title: Three accused Identified in Mandar Hill harassment case
articles.summary: Police identify three suspects in Mandar Hill harassment and extortion case in Banka after viral video; FIR filed under BNS and IT Act; raids underway to arrest.
articles.body: Patna: Police have identified three youths accused of allegedly harassing, threatening and extorting money from a girl and her friends at Mandar Hill in Banka district, after a video of the incident surfaced online on Sept 22. An FIR has been registered and raids are underway to arrest the accused, said police.According to police, the incident occurred on June 3 but came to light after the video went viral. The footage was brought to the notice of Bounsi police through WhatsApp on Sept 22. A team led by Bounsi SHO Pankaj Kumar verified that the video was shot at Mandar Hill, a popular tourist destination.Police said the girl had visited the hill with two friends when the accused allegedly stopped them, misbehaved with her, abused the trio and threatened them. One of the accused, identified as Abdullah, allegedly forced one of the girl’s friends to transfer Rs 1,500 online before letting them leave.While some youths have been detained for questioning, the three named accused remain absconding. Police initially registered a case against unidentified persons and later identified the accused using the viral video and other evidence. The victim’s statement was recorded on Friday.Banka SP Amitesh Kumar said the accused seen in the footage had been identified and raids were underway to apprehend them. “Police are examining all aspects of the case and further action will be taken based on the evidence collected. An FIR has been registered at Bounsi police station under relevant sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) and the Information Technology Act. articles.title: Noida bus fire: Families struggle to identify charred bodies, use anklet, other clues; 6 named
articles.summary: NOIDA: For families of the nine people killed when a sleeper bus caught fire on the Yamuna Expressway, the tragedy deepened at a Sector 94 post-mortem
articles.body: NOIDA: For families of the nine people killed when a sleeper bus caught fire on the Yamuna Expressway, the tragedy deepened at a Sector 94 post-mortem house on Friday, where relatives struggled to identify their loved ones because of the extensive burns.Police have so far identified six of the nine deceased.The bus, travelling from Kashmere Gate in Delhi to Mahoba in Uttar Pradesh, caught fire around 11.20pm on Wednesday near the 33-km milestone of the expressway, killing nine passengers, according to officials.At the Sector 94 post-mortem house, relatives waited anxiously as they tried to identify the bodies.Among them was Sarvagya, son of Rekha Bhardwaj, an injured passenger who survived the incident.Rekha had been travelling with her husband, Devendra Sahay Bhardwaj, who died in the fire.Sarvagya said his father, a retired teacher from a university in Hisar, Haryana, and his mother were travelling to Mahoba to attend the last rites of his grandmother.Siblings Shivam and Nancy also spent hours at the mortuary after learning about the bus fire.They eventually identified the bodies of their mother and brother after considerable difficulty and were seen consoling each other while waiting for officials to complete the formalities.In another case, Ayushi, the granddaughter of one of the deceased, identified the body with the help of an anklet that had been gifted by her son, highlighting the difficulties families faced in identifying victims because of the extensive burns.Police have identified six of the deceased as Shruti Rawat, 31, a resident of Chhatarpur in Madhya Pradesh; Saroj Gupta, 52, and Mayank Gupta, 28, both residents of Mughalpuria Bazar in Rath, Hamirpur; Devendra Sahay Bhardwaj, 60, a resident of Chandra Nagar village in Hisar, Haryana; Har Sharan Gupta, 55, a resident of Balaji Palace in Rajendra Nagar under Orai police station in Jalaun district; and Usha Devi, 65, a resident of Main Road, Muskura, Hamirpur.Police have arrested two drivers and a conductor in connection with the incident. The drivers were identified as Pawan and Yogesh Dixit, both residents of Kanpur Dehat, while the conductor was identified as Rohit, also a resident of Kanpur Dehat.During interrogation, the accused told police that they were travelling from Kashmere Gate to Mahoba on Wednesday night. They allegedly abandoned the vehicle and fled after it suddenly caught fire.An FIR has been registered under BNS Sections 281 (rash driving), 125(b) (endangering life) and 105 (culpable homicide), among others, police said.Rajesh Mohan, a Public Transport Officer with the Gautam Buddh Nagar Regional Transport Office, told PTI that the bus had accumulated fines totalling Rs 1.75 lakh through 19 challans.The bus is operated by Raj Kalpana Travel Agency of Madhya Pradesh but is registered in Madhubani, Bihar, the official said.Additional District Magistrate Ajeet Kumar Singh said on Thursday that the fire was caused by a short circuit and that 35 passengers were onboard, nine of whom died.The injured passengers were provided first aid before being transported to Mahoba in a special vehicle, Singh said.(With PTI inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Noida | Silver Rate in Noida | Bank Holidays in Noida | Public Holidays in Noida | Noida AQI | Weather in Noida | Petrol Price in Noida | Diesel Price in Noida | CNG Price in Noida | LPG Price in NoidaStay updated with the latest Noida news.
